findings.message: The Python block parser keeps reading lines until one does not start with `# `. It never stops after the header line plus seven key lines. When a file's body starts with a comment right after the docstring (or at the top of a file with no docstring), for example `# section` or `# noqa ...`, `refresh` inserts a valid block that is followed by that comment. The next `parse` reads the comment as part of the block, sees more than seven key lines and raises `Malformed`. As a result, `check` reports a file that `refresh` just wrote as `malformed`, and a second `refresh` refuses it with exit 2. A file's own leading comments therefore make it impossible to annotate.
findings.paved_road: Read exactly `len(KEYS)` lines after `# clutch:meta`. Each must start with `# `, or the block is malformed. Treat everything after them as body. Add a unit test in `tests/unit/test_meta_refresh.py` for a Python file whose body starts with a `# comment` line: refresh it, then check that `parse` succeeds and a second refresh returns `([], [])`.

findings.message: The `meta refresh` refusal prints only `clutch meta refresh: <path>: malformed`. It has no ` -- <what to do instead>` part. `docs/how-clutch-works.md` section 2 says every refusal prints `clutch <verb>: <message> -- <what to do instead>`, and the fail-closed rule requires a refusal to say what to do next.
findings.paved_road: Add a next step to the message, for example `... -- fix or remove the block so it has schema plus the six keys with a valid kind, then rerun clutch meta refresh`.

findings.message: The new `meta` row has two cells, but the table has three columns (`Verb | Works while serve runs? | What it does`). The description lands in the 'Works while serve runs?' column and the row says nothing about whether `meta` can run while serve runs.
findings.paved_road: Split it into two rows with three cells each: `meta refresh` | No | ... (it takes the writer lock) and `meta check` | Yes | ... (read-only).
